criterion_notes.c1: Fails C1: This is a methodological article on collecting, validating ('groundtruthing'), and analyzing crowd-sourced data in comparative politics, drawing illustratively on companion studies (Hyun et al. 2018; Kumar et al. 2018) of NextDrop's SMS water-arrival alert system in Bangalore. It examines crowd-sourced data quality and frontline workers' data-reporting compliance rather than household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain reading vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper discusses governance and administrative factors (street-level bureaucracy, principal-agent oversight in a state-owned water utility, and an MOU/job-description mandate instructing valvemen to report valve openings to NextDrop), so it would pass Criterion 2 on plain wording alone (though plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because the paper fails C1 and C4). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, it fails C2 ('no'): requiring valvemen to phone in valve opening times to a third-party SMS notification platform is an informational/transparency reporting tool to help households cope with intermittency, not a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation requirements, tariffs, disconnection/enforcement, or SLB discretion over who receives water—which PDF Page 16 explicitly defers to future research).
criterion_notes.c3: Passes C3: Although primarily a methodological synthesis drawing on companion empirical papers (Hyun et al. 2018; Kumar et al. 2017/2018), the article reports empirical groundtruthing methods and descriptive findings from Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board subdivision E3, including comparisons of valveman notifications against official schedules and a two-round 3,000-household geo-referenced survey, ethnographic shadowing of 9 valvemen over 4 months, and a small telephone survey of NextDrop users.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails C4: Reports no outcome measuring household or community water access, connection, service availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. The only empirical outcomes reported are valvemen's compliance (~70% submitting regularly) and accuracy (at least two-thirds inaccurate) in logging notifications with NextDrop, the association of valvemen's family/financial burdens with reporting compliance, neighbor sharing of SMS alerts, and which actors low-income respondents contact regarding complaints (>60% valvemen vs. <10% local leaders/councilors). Household welfare/access impacts from the 120-cluster trial are not reported here.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails C5 for review scope: While the underlying Bangalore fieldwork samples are described (valvemen and 3,000 surveyed households in 120 clusters), no exposure-outcome relationship governing household or community water/sanitation service access is analyzed or reported in this methodological article.

evidence_quotes.quote: In this paper, we draw on our own research on the politics of urban water delivery in India to highlight new types of analysis that are possible using crowd-sourced data and propose solutions to common pitfalls associated with analyzing it.
As a part of an impact evaluation of NextDrop’s services, our research team fielded a two-round 3000 household survey in Bangalore utility subdivision E3.

There, NextDrop entered a formal MOU with the state water utility, which instructed the valvemen’s supervisors to cooperate with NextDrop. NextDrop delivered reports to valvemen’s supervisors on a weekly basis that detailed individual reporting rates, giving supervisors the information needed to enforce compliance.
in our study area, approximately 70% of valvemen submitted notifications regularly, but at least two-thirds of the notifications submitted were inaccurate.

Triangulating between the valveman reports, an original dataset on valveman and valve area characteristics, and qualitative research, we observed that valveman compliance was strongly associated with non-political factors, such as individual and family financial circumstances.
To what extent, for example, do SLBs like valvemen exercise autonomy in their decisions regarding to whom to allocate water or other services and when?

raw_response.exposure: NextDrop crowd-sourced water-timing notification system and a state water utility MOU/directive instructing frontline valvemen and supervisors to report valve opening and closing times (plus valvemen's personal financial and family circumstances)
raw_response.outcome: Valvemen's frequency and accuracy of submitting valve-timing notifications to NextDrop, citizen sharing of SMS alerts, and share of low-income survey respondents contacting valvemen versus local leaders/councilors with water complaints (no water service access, availability, reliability, or affordability outcomes reported)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Water utility frontline workers (valvemen, including 9 shadowed for 4 months) and households (two-round 3,000-household survey across 120 valve-area clusters) in Bangalore utility subdivision E3, India
raw_response.rationale: Exclude (E01: Wrong topic; also fails C2 under the narrow rule-type reading and fails C4 under all readings). This article is a methodological overview on collecting, groundtruthing, and designing experiments around crowd-sourced data for comparative politics research, drawing illustratively on two companion studies of NextDrop's SMS water-timing alert system in Bangalore, India (Hyun et al. 2018; Kumar et al. 2018). First, its topic is crowd-sourced data methodology rather than household or community water service access (C1 = no). Second, under the 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification of Criterion 2, the utility MOU requiring valvemen to phone in valve opening times to an external notification app is an informational reporting mandate, not a rule-type mechanism governing service access, and street-level bureaucratic discretion over actual water allocation is explicitly left as a question for future research on p. 16 (C2 = no under narrow reading; passes plain C2 wording as bureaucratic principal-agent analysis, but plain_criterion2_decision is still 'exclude' due to C1 and C4). Third, the paper reports no water access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes—only valvemen's notification submission rates and accuracy (~70% reporting, >=2/3 inaccurate) and citizen complaint-contacting channels (C4 = no).
raw_response.study_design: Methodological overview illustrating mixed-methods groundtruthing (crowd-sourced reports, two-round 3,000-household geo-referenced survey, 120-cluster trial design description, and 4-month shadowing of 9 valvemen) drawn from companion studies
